Consumer spending has become unhinged from labor market income. People often cite the virtuous circle of growth, real income growth and real consumer spending. Not right now. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 January 2026 ab 28 Cold weather—the survey week was colder than normal We expect seasonably cold weather shaved ~25K off of the headline gain in nonfarm payroll employment in December. Weather turned unseasonably cold, and at the onset of winter which risks seasonal layoffs leaving employment sooner than normal. In addition, in empirical tests, and even weighting the sample toward more post-2020 years, cold in December does appear to matter. The reason one would test for December explicitly is because we have seen a general dampening of the impact of the seasons on employment flows. The weather effects ranged from -6K to -70K in our empirical models, with averages, medians and the most stable coefficients implying a hit of roughly 25K. Hot mix asphalt requires temperatures above 50 degrees to cure adequately otherwise it cools too quickly and will be less durable, and cold mix asphalt becomes difficult to work with when temperatures fall below 40 degrees. A number of different types of outdoor labor often idle for cold snaps or seasonal businesses shutter when temperatures drop below a certain point. On the Monday of the week including the 12th, December 8, temperatures were already low enough to see high temperatures below 40 degrees in Washington, DC when near 50 is more normal. While our base case is for uncertainty to recede, we perceive an elevated risk of an abrupt, nonlinear cooling if changes in trade policy keep coming. Meanwhile, we think the FOMC’s stated intention to move policy close to 3% would result in a stimulative stance that would likely leave inflation running at or above 3% indefinitely. ▪ Cyclical shock: Should the FOMC become convinced that the unemployment rate is likely to rise quickly and sharply, we think it would respond with a very aggressive monetary policy easing, such as three consecutive 50bp rate cuts. Recent data have toned down that risk. ▪ Structural shock: A structural shock could complicate matters. Recessionary growth and a steady unemployment rate – perhaps because of a larger decline in labor supply than our base case assumes – would likely limit room to loosen policy. If productivity surges (perhaps on account of AI), growth might remain strong even as the unemployment rate rises more than we expect. Rate cuts would likely follow, but would be ill-suited to mitigate AI-induced labor slackening. records.text: igating downward bias from October imputation The BLS clarified on Wednesday, and revised a FAQ update originally posted Tuesday, on CPI rent imputations. Initially, the BLS announced a procedure that would not allow October's imputed zero rent increase to fully reverse in April. That would have implied a permanent downward bias from the calculation of rents. On Wednesday, the BLS revised the FAQ and the BLS staff clarified that "Effects of the carry-forward imputation method utilized in October 2025 will resolve in April 2026 when that housing panel is used again," see here. That should allow the effects of the October rent imputations to be unwound in the April CPI and avoid permanently biasing lower the index level. FOMC Minutes: Not that hawkish Overall, the December FOMC meeting minutes revealed most FOMC participants got on board with the December rate cut, without all that much resistance. The minutes also say that most FOMC participants expect to keep lowering rates in 2026 as long as inflation moves down in line with expectations. That would be consistent with the economic projections and assumptions of appropriate policy submitted for that meeting's Summary of Economic Projections. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 January 2026 ab 45 Note that this year, the FRB of New York inflation expectations measures did not rise to the same degree as expectations in the University of Michigan survey. This could be partly related to recent methodology changes impacting the University of Michigan measure (see our analysis here) and the fact that the surveys are measuring expectations on a different basis. Expectations in both series sit well off the peaks seen in April and May of this year. We expect continued sogginess in FRB of New York respondents' labor market expectations in December, abstracting from some month-to-month movements up and down. Despite some slight improvement at the margins, the November data indicated that respondents' concern about the labor market persists. The mean perceived probability of finding a job in the next three months if one loses a job retraced its October decline, rising 0.6 pp to 47.4%, but remained well below its 12-month average of 50.6%. The mean perceived probability of leaving one's job voluntarily fell 1.1 pp to 17.7%, 2 pp below the 2024 average, suggesting that workers are hesitant to separate by choice. Expectations that the unemployment rate would be higher in a year's time fell 0.5 pp to 42.1%, but the series still sits well above the 36.5% 2024 average. Gross EGB supply to reach €1.5trn in 2026 Based on the funding outlooks released by national treasuries, we project overall gross EGB supply at a new record level of c.€1.5trn in 2026, increasing by close to €100bn y/y. Redemptions are also set to increase by c.€100bn y/y, to above €900bn; in that context net bond issuance should be little-changed y/y at close to €600bn. Gross and net issuance volumes will remain far above the levels seen in the pre-pandemic era, reflecting still-elevated budget deficits (our economists project the aggregate euro area budget deficit at c.3.5% in 2026, modestly above 2025's c.3.3% level and far above pre-pandemic lows close to 0.5%). Particularly with EGB redemptions remaining elevated beyond 2026, gross EGB issuance volumes are likely to stay high for years to come in the absence of material fiscal consolidation. On top of net issuance from DMOs, the ECB appears set to continue adding to the net supply burden via full-pace QT next year: as such, we pencil in net issuance post-QT close to €870bn (Figure 1). records.text: Oil market implications Amarpreet Singh BCI, US Maduro's apprehension and the beginning of a political transition has raised the prospect of a potential recovery in the country's oil output, which has been weighed down by lack of investments due to political challenges for more than two decades. The situation remains fluid and this is likely the first step in a long process that could lead to long-term policy stability for the oil sector, which will be crucial in driving the much-needed private investments. However, assuming a relatively smooth transition, we expect a 200-300 kb/d increase in the country's oil output through the end of 2026 and a 1 mb/d gain by the end of the decade from current levels of ~1 mb/d. For markets, we think this will likely translate into a $2-3/b downside over the near term and a somewhat thinner right tail over the medium term. There is historical precedent for a reopening and a renationalization of the oil sector in Venezuela. Following the reforms in the early 1990s, which led to private investments in unconventional development in the Orinoco belt, the country's oil output increased from 2.2 mb/d in 1990 to 3.2 mb/d in 2000. Signpost 3: Deviation in IOR from the monetary policy stance Under the Federal Reserve Act, authority to pay interest on reserves (IOR) is assigned to the Board. There is no requirement for the Board to move IOR in accordance with the FOMC’s monetary policy stance, although it has consistently done so in the past. In the event of a severe breakdown in collegiality at the Fed, it is in theory possible that the Board could force interest rates lower by reducing IOR below the level proposed by FOMC in its policy statement . In the FOMC's Implementation Note after the September meeting, the word "unanimously“ was removed with respect to a vote of the Board of Governors to change the interest on reserves rate. records.text: 2026 Inflation Outlook: Traveling Toward Target After reaching a peak of 5.6% three years ago, core PCE inflation had returned most of the way back to the 2% target by 2024. Progress on inflation was limited in 2025: we forecast core PCE inflation of 2.7% for Dec. 2025 vs. 3.0% for Dec. 2024. However, most of the remaining overshoot and 0.3pp upside surprise relative to our year-ago forecast appears to reflect the one-time impact of larger than expected tariffs, rather than firmer underlying cost pressures. While distortions are likely to boost the next two months of inflation readings, we expect near-target and below-consensus inflation in 2026 for three reasons: a smaller boost from tariffs, soft shelter inflation, and a cooler labor market. Nearly Back to the 2% Target by the End of 2026 We expect progress on disinflation to resume in 2026, for three reasons. First, we expect less of a boost to inflation from tariff-related price pressures. We estimate that tariff passthrough has contributed 0.5pp to year-over-year core PCE inflation, implying that inflation excluding the impact of tariffs has already fallen to 2.3%. Our estimate of the impact of tariffs on inflation so far is slightly smaller than estimates from the Fed Board staff, St. Louis Fed economists, and the Harvard Pricing Lab. records.text: M Idea 2 CPI: April shelter payback and December upward bias confirmed The Bureau of Labor Statistics has provided new details that resolve earlier uncertainty and confirm significant distortions ahead. First, the April 2026 shelter payback is now officially confirmed. After some back-and- forth the BLS updated their FAQ with the following: "Effects of the carry-forward imputation method utilized in October 2025 will resolve in April 2026 when that housing panel is used again. The 1-month rent change estimated for April 2026 will be atypical: it will essentially be based on the 1/6th root of 12-month change, instead of the 1/6th root of a 6-month change." This clarification matters because under normal circumstances, shelter inflation is calculated by taking the six-month change in rents and dividing by six, effectively smoothing the adjustment across months. The missed October observation created a gap that now compresses a full year’s change into the standard formula, producing an outsized April print. This confirms the payback we anticipated and suggests April shelter CPI will likely show a sharp increase, adding meaningful upward pressure to core CPI. We estimate a +10bp upward bias to core CPI in April 2026. The BLS also addressed the treatment of bi-monthly pricing and confirmed an upward bias for December. records.text: 2026 Inflation Outlook: Traveling Toward Target After reaching a peak of 5.6% three years ago, core PCE inflation had returned most of the way back to the 2% target by 2024. Progress on inflation was limited in 2025: we forecast core PCE inflation of 2.7% for Dec. 2025 vs. 3.0% for Dec. 2024. However, most of the remaining overshoot and 0.3pp upside surprise relative to our year-ago forecast appears to reflect the one-time impact of larger than expected tariffs, rather than firmer underlying cost pressures. While distortions are likely to boost the next two months of inflation readings, we expect near-target and below-consensus inflation in 2026 for three reasons: a smaller boost from tariffs, soft shelter inflation, and a cooler labor market. Nearly Back to the 2% Target by the End of 2026 We expect progress on disinflation to resume in 2026, for three reasons. First, we expect less of a boost to inflation from tariff-related price pressures. We estimate that tariff passthrough has contributed 0.5pp to year-over-year core PCE inflation, implying that inflation excluding the impact of tariffs has already fallen to 2.3%. Our estimate of the impact of tariffs on inflation so far is slightly smaller than estimates from the Fed Board staff, St. Louis Fed economists, and the Harvard Pricing Lab. records.text: K Debt Management Office Our working assumption is that the £255bn net financing requirement will be met by £15bn increase in the bill stock and £240bn in gilt sales. This would be the lowest outright level since FY22/23. We assume a breakdown of £95bn each in shorts and mediums, £10bn in longs and £15bn in linkers with a residual £25bn in unallocated supply. Our central view is that there will be no long conventional supply via auctions with the DMO holding two syndications of longs over the course of the programme and instead, meeting any demand for longs via its tender programme. The DMO needs to create genuine scarcity in the long end of the conventional curve – what we have termed a "supplier's strike" and a reduced financing need provides an opportunity to do so and de-emphasise the importance of 30y gilt yields which have come to be the lightning conductor for fiscal malcontent. While this might seem like a big step, in terms of percentage of overall supply, it would only be reducing the percentage share of longs and linkers by 5pp and 4pp respectively from their Budget 2025 levels (Figure 34). records.text: Tepid fiscal salvo might deepen Fed cuts in recession risk case 8023 January 2026 ▪ While we think the risk of a US recession has decreased, we also see less space for an aggressive fiscal policy response if o ne occurs (see US: Downgrade is another step towards unpredictability , dated May 2025). ▪ In the event of a recession, lawmakers could choose to hold back on fiscal stimulus, constrained by either ‘bond vigilantes’ or a ‘bond-vigilant’ administration. This is a process that could take at least six months to a year until it's feasible for new elections to be held. In order to have a credible election, at the very least, a new National Electoral Council (CNE) might have to be appointed and international observers would have to be involved, which would require time to conduct the necessary due process. Moreover, a negotiated process would likely require the introduction of legal reforms to provide guarantees and protection to the ruling elite before any potential transfer of power happens. We should also note that within a relevant range there appears to be a fair amount compression to a trend that is also above our model estimates. This is akin to noting how adaptive a seasonal factor can be. Or, upon initial release of the data, how much of any innovation is deemed an evolving seasonal pattern that needs to be offset by seasonal adjustment. That's what happened in November, which we note above. November was compressed toward the trend in private at ~70K SA, or the trend assessed by the seasonal adjustment filters. The opposite happened in December 2024. The NSA strength ended up leading seasonal adjustment to assess a new trend was emerging and provide much less support as a result. Compression looks particularly onerous for the NSA changes below what would be consistent with a zero SA change. In our simulations, compression increases at an increasing rate as NSA changes move below a range consistent with an SA change of roughly 60K. records.text: Long-term rates could destabilize after successive periods of high inflation 6423 January 2026 ▪ The 1960s and 1970s were a story of successive positive shocks to inflation, which occurred in a period of generally tight la bor markets. The FOMC at the time saw these shocks as transitory and reacted to them in what it thought was a measured way. ▪ Taking place in a period of profound economic and social change and rising general distrust in government, the cumulative eff ect of these shocks was a significant rise in long -term interest rates (LTIR). This brought about entrenched inflation and eventually a costl y effort by the Volcker-era FOMC to reduce it. ▪ The FOMC is faced with a somewhat similar policy context: deciding on monetary policy immediately after a period of high infl ation, with inflation still above target and a risk that it reaccelerates in the event of an exogenous shock. 1970s show the risk of losing the inflation anchor Sources: Reis (2021), BEA, BLS, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Sources: FRB New York, University of Michigan, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Inflation expectations continue to be at risk due to tariffs

We assume gross issuance in the middle of this range, which would imply net bond issuance of c.€13bn (c.€9bn lower y/y). • Bill stock to grow modestly: Regarding short-term funding tools, the funding plan pencils in an increase in the stock of €2-4bn, whereas in 2025 the stock shrank by c.€3bn. • WAM of debt stock likely to drift lower: The DMO has set an end-2026 portfolio tenor target range of 10.25-11.75yrs, versus c.11.5yrs estimated at the end of 2025. In recent commentary the head of the Austrian DMO has signalled that the WAM of the debt stock is likely to decline from current levels, as mentioned above. • Syndications: The funding plan states that three deals will be placed. We expect Austria's first syndication of the year to come in the form of a 10y benchmark launch in January (this could potentially be accompanied by syndicated taps at other tenors). As for the remaining syndications, we think the second one is likely to be placed in the spring (April/May), with the third potentially coming at the end of the summer (or in early autumn). records.text: Signpost 1: Altering the operations of the regional reserve banks The Fed Board is authorized to oversee the operations of the regional reserve banks, and if used aggressively, this could allow for discharging reserve bank presidents and senior staff at any time. Notably, all reserve bank presidents serve five-year terms that expire at the end of February in years ending in 1 or 6 – making February 2026 a key deadline . A majority of Board members must ratify any extension of those appointments. As a “no” vote has never happened in the Fed’s 112-year history, denial of extension for any regional reserve bank presidents would be alarming. This would especially be the case for the New York Fed, given that monetary policy operations are run day-to-day from the branch’s Markets Group. Signpost 2: Sweeping changes to formulation of monetary policy An administration Board majority would also have plenary authority to discharge members of the Board staff, including the leadership of its economics and monetary policy teams. Some amount of turnover at the Fed is normal in transition – for example, some staff leadership on the regulatory side has occurred following Governor Bowman’s assumption of the role of Vice Chair for Supervision . However, the day-to-day use of Board authority to require voting on policy in a certain way or to dramatically reshape the Fed’s staff could cause markets to doubt the decentralized, well-understood approach historically used at the central bank to form

records.text: In the special questions in this month’s Dallas Fed surveys, more firms indicated that they were currently using artificial intelligence (AI) than when the question was last asked in May, and most reported that AI has not impacted their need for workers so far. 67% of firms reported that they were currently using traditional AI, generative AI, or both, compared to 59% when the question was last asked in May. 76% of firms reported that the use of AI has not impacted their need for workers, while 10% reported that AI had changed the type but not the number of workers needed, 8% reported that AI had reduced their need for workers, and 3% reported that it had increased their need for workers. Looking ahead, 60% of firms expected AI to have no impact on the number of workers needed over the next few years, while 25% of firms expected AI to reduce their need for workers in the medium term. Firms whose employment has been impacted by the use of AI reported that low-skill workers and workers with little or no work experience had been the most negatively impacted on net. Portugal (2026: c.€24bn, +c.€2bn vs 2025) • The Portuguese DMO published its 2026 funding plan on 15 December 2025, pencilling in total gross PGB issuance of c.€24bn (an upside surprise versus our previous projection of €18bn). In addition, MTN issuance is projected to total €2.5bn, with close to €1bn raised from retail funding instruments (our 2026 bond issuance profile does not include these latter funding sources, given uncertainty around timing). • Bill stock to increase significantly: With respect to t-bills, the funding plan indicates that net t-bill issuance should total c.€5bn, whereas in 2025 net t-bill issuance was negative to the tune of c.-€1bn. • Syndications: The funding plan states that three syndications will be placed next year. We expect Portugal to begin its syndication programme with the launch of a 10y benchmark in January, as in previous years. records.text: For January, we tentatively forecast monthly core PCE of 0.27% and core CPI of 0.26%, reflecting a modest boost from outsized start of the year price increases (i.e., what we’ve dubbed the “January effect”). The left panel of Exhibit 10 shows that for the last three years, inflation has been higher at the start of the year, and in particular in January. We wouldn’t expect a January acceleration of the same magnitude as in prior years because price pressures have moderated, the bar for a seasonally adjusted January jump has been raised as the seasonal factors have come to expect larger January increases, and a hotter December reading raises the bar for an acceleration. But we are still penciling in a January effect-driven boost in January core PCE inflation of 8bp because the level of inflation has yet to fully normalize and it is possible that some companies will use January price resetting as an opportunity to pass on a larger share of past tariff costs than in surrounding months (Exhibit 10, right). records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 02 January 2026 Citi Research 2 The summary of deliberations from the BoC’s December decision to hold policy rates at 2.25% was a bit more hawkish than we expected, but ultimately not too surprising and with nothing to change our expectations that conditions will warrant more rate cuts in 2026. The most notable new development in the discussion of policy rates is that officials are unsure if the next move in rates will be higher or lower: “Governing Council members also discussed whether it was more likely that their next move would be to raise or lower the policy interest rate. Given the high level of uncertainty, members agreed that while the current policy rate was at about the right level in the current situation, it was difficult to predict when and in which direction the next change in the policy rate would be. ” While consistent with market pricing for rates through 2026, acknowledging the potential for future hikes is a bit more hawkish than we would have expected at this stage. Still, the lack of guidance clearly leaves the chance for more cuts on the table. If anything, given that officials see the current level of policy rates as being on the accommodative end of neutral, and that forecasts expect a closing of the output gap over the next year with rates at 2.25%, the next move in their baseline should be toward higher rates. Spending has slowed, but real spending still grew a solid 2.6% over the last four quarters, despite real disposable income growth rising just 1.5% over the same period. • Households across all income groups expect to be more sensitive to future inflation now than in 2022. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 January 2026 ab 8 Estimating the Fed's reaction function We published this two weeks ago but with some questions on interpreting the weights we reprinted the analysis this week. Essentially, with the year coming to a close we updated our analysis of the FOMC reaction function, and the weights being placed on inflation versus the labor market in the setting of monetary policy. The results were somewhat surprising and do not suggest a high bar to more rate cuts to come. Many clients argue that the FOMC is being too dovish. Or, they note the FOMC has shifted too far to prioritizing the labor market. We spent a lot of 2025 writing about Chair Powell's risk management framework. However, when we look at the data, the FOMC has merely gone from ignoring the labor market to putting it on more equal footing, as their legal mandate suggests. In their latest interpretation of their goals, the FOMC writes " if the Committee judges that the objectives are not complementary, it follows a balanced approach in promoting them." We use the assumptions of appropriate policy or so called "dot plot" to trace out the evolution of the FOMC reaction function and find that the FOMC has roughly set the funds rate in line with what the data implies and has merely put inflation and full employment on equal footing. records.text: sonal consumption expenditures expanded a brisk 2.6% during those 4 quarters. The wealth effect from rising equities has been pretty extraordinary. People accuse us of underestimating it but looking across other projections, we would argue that's pretty widespread. Most other forecasters had stronger labor markets and labor income than we did, so to the extent others were surprised on the downside by labor income, they too were probably surprised on the upside by the wealth effect. We write extensively on the topic in US: SCOTUS vs. IEEPA, dated November 2025. Broadly speaking, we see three potential rulings: 1. Full affirmation: SCOTUS finds that IEEPA authorizes the administration’s broad -based reciprocal tariffs, sustaining the current regime and strengthening executive power. 2. Partial approval: SCOTUS may allow limited tariffs under IEEPA, such as only for a defined set of goods or for countries that are linked to a genuine emergency nexus (e.g. Chinese fentanyl or a specific cybersecurity supply chain risk). In effect, SCOTUS would b e saying the president can use IEEPA in such instances because it deals with an emergency as defined, but would simultaneously reject broader tariffs that lack a close causal connection to that emergency. 3. Reversal: SCOTUS upholds the view of lower courts that IEEPA does not support broad tariffs, effectively striking them down. records.text: 2 Natasha Kaneva AC (1-212) 834-3175 natasha.kaneva@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 04 January 2026 J P M O R G A N Looking ahead, we continue to maintain our view that a regime change in Venezuela would immediately represent one of the largest upside risks to the global oil supply outlook for 2026–2027 and beyond (Barrels behind barriers—Venezuela and Russia, 19 December 2025). Impact on production: Venezuela could realistically increase output by 500-600 kbd within two years In a post-Maduro scenario, however, the transition itself could potentially trigger a short, sharp shock. Historical precedent—such as the 2002–2003 PDVSA strike—suggests that production could temporarily fall by as much as 50%, due to operational disruptions, workforce dislocation, or precautionary shutdowns across PDVSA facilities (Figure 1). Beyond this initial dip, however, the recovery is expected to be swift. With a stable political environment, renewed licensing, restored diluent flows, and unrestricted Chevron operations, supply could rapidly rebound to around 1.2 mbd within a few months. Given that average supply in recent months has hovered around 900–950 kbd, this scenario presents a potential uplift of 250 kbd compared to the 2025 average. The risks to our inflation forecasts, both those posed by policy and the economic cycle, appear more balanced this year. In particular, unlike last year, tariffs pose two-sided risks. On the upside, tariff rates could rise, against our expectation, or the share of tariff costs borne by US consumers could rise with a longer lag beyond the 70% peak we assume. On the downside, the effective tariff rate could decline if, for example, exemptions become more prevalent or the Supreme Court strikes down the IEEPA-based tariffs and the administration does not replace a meaningful share of those tariffs using different authorities. Hotter Inflation Prints in December and January While we generally expect benign inflation this year, distortions are likely to boost the next two monthly readings. For December, we tentatively forecast monthly core PCE inflation of 0.25% and core CPI of 0.28%, reflecting the unwind of the negative impact of delayed data collection that depressed measured prices in November. Because the government shutdown extended through the middle of November, a disproportionate share of the prices in CPI were collected in late November, a period of steep holiday discounting (Exhibit 9, left). records.text: US Economics Weekly 02 January 2026 Citi Research 8 JOLTS Job Openings – Citi: 7785k, median: 7763k, prior: 7670k JOLTS job openings were surprisingly stronger in September and October and may increase modestly again in November to 7785k. This would be in line with job postings on Indeed.com that also moved up at the start of the month. However, we would caution that job postings last year also exhibited the same residual seasonality patterns that have led to stronger jobs data later in the year. In general, JOLTS job openings, which never fell back to pre-pandemic levels over the last few years, have not been a good indication of actual demand for workers. The more important details in the JOLTS report will be the labor market flows. In October, hiring and quit rates were very low while the layoff rate ticked up slightly but to a still-low level. Revisions to October data will be made to align JOLTS flows with October payrolls and could mean larger quits or other separations in October, reflecting a larger drag from federal government employment. Solid payroll job growth in November could imply hiring rates stabilize, although at still relatively low levels. Given seasonal patterns in JOLTS hiring, we would not expect payroll job growth to slow again due to low hiring until around March/April. records.text: Low public confidence in the inflation target makes further easing risky 2223 January 2026 ▪ In an environment with shakily anchored inflation expectations, we think that easing monetary policy while tariff-fueled inflation is on the rise would pose risks that the FOMC would be hesitant to accept. ▪ Since the start of the pandemic, long-term inflation expectations have risen and are nearing 1990s highs. records.text: 1/3/2026 Buy the Dip, in spot and volatility Tactically, our delta view for Q1 is bullish: Historically, early warning signs in corporate earnings preceded the burst of valuation-bubbles. If earnings forecast revisions turn negative, it would be a red flag. Currently the opposite trend is evident. Consensus for 2026 was already for double digit growth going into Q3. It saw further upgrades following an exceptionally strong reporting season. Macro continues to be run hot. Fiscal is supportive. We expect record high tax refunds in Q1. The incoming Fed Chair could also give a Dovish impulse ahead of November's mid-terms. We anticipate elevated volatility: 2025 delivered a warning. The US equity market is now in a regime of rapid repeating mini-volatility cycles. Market structure has created a more fragile environment. The regime quickly shifts from volatility suppression, to violent unwinds, back to rapid mean-reversion. The underlying macro-fundamental cycle is also bullish for volatility. Leverage and consequently volatility are on the rise. Equity markets are trading in a valuation bubble. History tells us this creates fat tails on both sides of the distribution. Previous bubbles suggest understanding market structure can be one the most critical inputs for navigating convexity. We expect the funds rate is headed lower in 2026, with risks to our forecast of 0.5 pp of rate cuts tilted to the downside. In the US, there is a lot to look forward to. In 2026, the US, Mexico and Canada host a worldwide soccer tournament . The US celebrates the 250th anniversary of declaring independence from Great Britain. The nation's highest ever ranked men's and women's ice hockey teams head to the winter Olympics (yes, we know success is not guaranteed). At a headline level, everything looks fine. We are forecasting 2% real GDP growth next year, on the low end of consensus but not bad. Fiscal support, with bumper tax refund checks, and some very, very modest relief from lagged interest rate reductions should put a floor under the labor market slowdown. This tipped US equities firmly into an earnings contraction cycle. Which accelerated with the likes of Oracle and Cisco joining the sequence of profit warnings in early 2001. By the time the US economy entered a recession in March 2001, the NDX had already halved. Heading into 2026, the earnings outlook is very different: The Q3 2025 reporting season drove strong earnings upgrades with revisions at four-year highs. Momentum is robust at both ends of the barbell. Mega-cap Tech is seeing large upgrades along with small-caps and mid-caps. This is in stark contrast to the series of profit warnings seen in the late 1990s TMT bubble. We think the market is set up for a bullish start to the year with Q4 2025 earnings season kicking off in January’s second week. The risks to our inflation forecasts, both those posed by policy and the economic cycle, appear more balanced this year. In particular, unlike last year, tariffs pose two-sided risks. On the upside, tariff rates could rise, against our expectation, or the share of tariff costs borne by US consumers could rise with a longer lag beyond the 70% peak we assume. On the downside, the effective tariff rate could decline if, for example, exemptions become more prevalent or the Supreme Court strikes down the IEEPA-based tariffs and the administration does not replace a meaningful share of those tariffs using different authorities. Hotter Inflation Prints in December and January While we generally expect benign inflation this year, distortions are likely to boost the next two monthly readings. For December, we tentatively forecast monthly core PCE inflation of 0.25% and core CPI of 0.28%, reflecting the unwind of the negative impact of delayed data collection that depressed measured prices in November. Because the government shutdown extended through the middle of November, a disproportionate share of the prices in CPI were collected in late November, a period of steep holiday discounting (Exhibit 9, left). records.text: Less dynamism in the labor market 4023 January 2026 ▪ Low hiring plus low layoffs is an uncomfortable state of affairs in the labor market. The former suggests low labor demand, which could in turn open the floodgates in the latter if the economic outlook deteriorates. ▪ We see reduced churn as in part payback for pandemic-era tightness, as businesses likely remain wary about cutting headcount in what is still a historically tight job market. The pandemic experience showed that once let go, workers might not be so easily replaced. ▪ Signs of lower labor demand have increased rate-cut chatter among Fed doves, notably Governor Waller. He has relied on a vacancy-rate framework in the past to argue that a further slip in the job openings rate is likely to entail higher unemployment (see chart at right). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 15 US outlook scenarios Exhibit 22: Morgan Stanley US Economics baseline and alternative outlooks for the US Economy: 2025, 2026, and 2027 Baseline: Emerging from policy uncertainty (60%) Productivity-driven upside (12.5%) Aggregate demand upside ( 12.5%) Mild recession (15%) GDP growth Tariffs and a slower labor market weigh on growth near-term, but real growth accelerates slightly in 2026 after a weaker first half. Real GDP grows 1.6% in 2025, 1.8% in 2026, and 2.0% in 2027. AI-related investment bears fruit sooner than anticipated and boosts productivity and growth. records.text: irmed an upward bias for December. Data collected on a bi-monthly schedule are typically carried forward during off-cycle months. That is, prices from cities surveyed during even months (“even” cities) are assumed unchanged in odd months. This implies that prices from even cities were assumed unchanged from August to September, following the normal methodology. The source of bias has to do with the fact that, given the lack of October data because of the shutdown, the BLS was forced to carry forward August prices in even cities until November. And this implies that the December one-month price change will effectively represent an August-to-December move. This mechanism introduces a temporary upward bias in December CPI for components exposed to bi-monthly sampling. These clarifications remove prior uncertainty and reinforce our expectation of volatility in both December and April prints. December should show a boost from bi-monthly categories, partially offsetting prior weakness, while April will deliver the shelter payback we initially projected. As we detailed in a note last week, we currently expect a bias of +8bp in December as payback from the downward bias we saw in October and November.

records.text: cative and for information purposes only Volatility in valuation bubbles: CAPE (cyclically adjusted PE) has topped 30x in only three cycles: 1929, 1999 and today. Both 1929 and 1999 exhibited very fat right tails. But in terms of volatility, they had little in common. When the bubble popped in 1929, our model VIX peaked at ~100. The crash was one of the most violent in US equity history. In contrast, the 1999 burst was one of the lowest-velocity bear markets on record. NDX had already halved before 9/11 without VIX exceeding 35. Equity bear markets tend to be much longer and deeper during economic recessions. But the most convex crashes are typically a function of leverage and positioning, rather than fundamentals. 1929 and 1987 were the two largest peaks in 100 years for our model VIX. But with very different triggers, regimes and outcomes. Both saw forced selling from leveraged investors trigger outsized moves. 1929 was a story of margin loans and forced selling from levered investment trusts. In 1987, it was portfolio insurance. For 2026, flows from CTAs, volatility target funds, levered ETFs and retail investors create a complex and potentially volatile mixture. records.text: Data Quality Concerns: Smaller Seasonal Distortions but Continued Collection Issues At times in 2025, investors focused more on concerns about the quality of data than on the data itself. We expect residual seasonality to be less of a concern in 2026 but data collection problems to persist. Two years ago, we introduced tests for three kinds of seasonal distortions that had appeared in monthly inflation data. First, the “January effect” described above. Second, unusual and extreme fluctuations caused by the pandemic could be misinterpreted as changes to seasonal patterns, leading to inappropriate revisions to the seasonal factors. Third, the pandemic disrupted some seasonal patterns, causing some price series to begin failing seasonality tests, earning them an undeserved exemption from seasonal adjustment even as the old patterns reemerged. As the level of inflation has declined and the largest pandemic-era price swings have moved further into the past, seasonal factors and the seasonal adjustment process have normalized for many categories. For example, the left panel of Exhibit 11 shows that the share of CPI categories that are seasonally adjusted has rebounded from its 2022-2023 lows. As a result, our estimates of the impact of these seasonal distortions on overall core inflation has declined substantially. records.text: 4 January 2026 US Economic Notes Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 2 Regarding the November JOLTS, aside from the usual focus on the private sector hiring, layoffs and quits rates , we will also pay attention to specific sectors that may be more exposed to immigration policy as there has been some unusual divergences in the job openings and quits rates – two series that typically move in tandem across the business cycle. Case in point, the October job openings rate for accommodations & food services (6.4%) had increased by 50bps since the beginning of the year . However, the quits rate for the aforementioned sector surged from 3.7% in January to 5.3% in June before plunging to 3.2% as of October. records.text: Protected Status (TPS) allows individuals to live and work in the US legally if their home countries are deemed unsafe due to circumstances such as natural disasters, wars, or other "extraordinary and temporary" conditions, according to the Department of Homeland Security. According to the National Immigration Forum (link here), as of March 31, 2025, there were approximately 1.3 million individuals with TPS living in the US. Since September, the Trump administration has terminated TPS for South Sudan and Myanmar, affecting ~3K individuals, and the 2021 designation for Venezuela, impacting 242K individuals. To date, the Trump administration has terminated or announced its intent to terminate TPS or over 1 million of the 1.3 million, with the most from Venezuela (~600K), Haiti (~330K) and Honduras (~50K). Several decisions are being challenged in court. The Supreme Court granted the administration's request to stay a lower-court ruling that had allowed ~350K Venezuelans (who received TPS under the 2023 re-designation) to maintain their status while litigation continues. The affected individuals would have lost TPS and reverted to their prior status effective November 7, posing downside risks to future months. So far this year, a few large employers have announced plans to identify or remove affected workers from their employ, such as Walmart (link here) and Disney (link here). We also take stock of the expansion's fragility. It's hard to get too bearish expecting a bumper tax refund season thanks to OBBBA. Partly as a result, optimism abounds. However, things could get bumpy along the way. We take a contrarian view, inside. The Economic Comment starts on page 3. The Week Ahead: A busy week We expect nonfarm payroll employment expanded 90K in December, held down by weather but supported substantially by residual seasonality that poses upside risks. The unemployment rate likely fell to 4.5%. More Fedspeak returns at this weekend's American Economic Association meetings, including FRB of Philadelphia President Paulson, among others. Lightweight vehicle sales likely edged up 0.2 million to 15.8 million (saar) in December. The usual run of labor market data will precede the employment report, including JOLTS, Challenger job cuts, and ADP's estimate of private payroll employment. We expect the ISM manufacturing composite continued to hover slightly below 50 in December, and the non-manufacturing composite likely continued to signal subdued growth. records.text: Data Quality Concerns: Smaller Seasonal Distortions but Continued Collection Issues At times in 2025, investors focused more on concerns about the quality of data than on the data itself. We expect residual seasonality to be less of a concern in 2026 but data collection problems to persist. Two years ago, we introduced tests for three kinds of seasonal distortions that had appeared in monthly inflation data. First, the “January effect” described above. Second, unusual and extreme fluctuations caused by the pandemic could be misinterpreted as changes to seasonal patterns, leading to inappropriate revisions to the seasonal factors. Third, the pandemic disrupted some seasonal patterns, causing some price series to begin failing seasonality tests, earning them an undeserved exemption from seasonal adjustment even as the old patterns reemerged. As the level of inflation has declined and the largest pandemic-era price swings have moved further into the past, seasonal factors and the seasonal adjustment process have normalized for many categories. For example, the left panel of Exhibit 11 shows that the share of CPI categories that are seasonally adjusted has rebounded from its 2022-2023 lows. As a result, our estimates of the impact of these seasonal distortions on overall core inflation has declined substantially. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 January 2026 ab 12 Tax season tracking: monitoring stimulus The One Big Beautiful Bill Act implemented tax changes retroactive to 2025. That means individuals can claim refunds against their 2025 income when they file their 2025 tax returns in 2026. Because the tax law changes were passed midyear, most individuals were unlikely to fully account for the changes by adjusting their withheld income. As a result, we expect larger than normal tax refunds sent to households in 2026. In addition, 2026 withholding tables will be adjusted for the tax changes in the OBBBA. Together, the changes should boost spending in 2026, with Q2 seeing the most support. Note however, in the national accounts, the Bureau of Economic Analysis may book some of the boost to personal income in Q1, however. Overall we expect OBBBA to boost the level of GDP by 0.45% by Q4 2026, before more of the legislation's cuts arrive. The individual tax cuts are part of that, but we also expect the business provisions are a net plus in 2026 too. Note that when we add in other aspects of fiscal policy, including state and local government, along with Biden-era lifts that are unwinding, we expect the total contribution to Q4/Q4 over growth in 2026 to be roughly 0.3 pp. We have seen a range of estimates for how strong the refund season might be this spring, from as low as $30 billion more than 2025 to as high as $100 billion. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 January 2026 ab 4 As a result, we expect the FOMC to keep moving the funds rate lower. However, we expect strong inflation gains in December, January, and February data released in January, February and March. That, combined with decent expectations for the December employment report, led us to push our expectations for 50 bp of rate cuts in 2026 into the second half of the year, one 25 bp rate cut in July and another in October. The new Fed Chair could inherit a tough spot: elevated inflation and weak labor market. If not for inflation, we would expect a weak January employment report, with sizeable downward revisions at the annual revision, and downward revisions to October and November job gains alongside further weakness in the household survey, to motivate a March rate cut. The claims data turning higher into the March meeting from the seasonal lows at the turn of the year could help provide corroborating evidence the labor market remains weak. We expect lingering unemployment and the soggy labor market to support the next Fed Chair in marshalling the FOMC into lowering rates, but after the H1 inflation scare subsides. Pricing the upside case: Despite all of the uncertainties, we have consistently used 35c as our upside case in the event of a political transition. In December, we introduced an upside case of 40c (Venezuela: Closer, but not there yet, December 9, 2025). In the following exercise, we will use 35c, 40c, and 45c as potential recovery values. We also make several simplifying assumptions: • All VENZ and PDVSA unsecured bonds will be treated as pari passu with one another • Past due interest (PDI) will be treated as pari passu with par claims If we assume that bonds immediately pull towards recovery values of 35c/40c/45c, we can expect unsecured VENZ and PDVSA bonds, on average, to rise 5.4c, 10.1c, and 14.9c, respectively. However, if we assume that the market prices in two years for a restructuring deal to be consummated (assuming a 6% discount rate), bonds might rally only 1.7c, 6.0c, and 10.2c, respectively. Figure 1 highlights the potential upside case for VENZ bonds under these various scenarios. Figure 2 suggests further upside for PDVSA bonds, which were still trading at a small discount to the VENZ complex as of January 2. Figure 3 provides a more comprehensive table of the unsecured bonds and our upside estimates. 4 January 2026 7 Barclays | Venezuela
